##### **1.4 Graphical Kinematics and Feature Extraction from Curves** Kinematic trajectories are analyzed graphically by establishing differential and integral correspondences across three vertically aligned coordinate graphs: position $x(t)$ (or distance $S(t)$), velocity $v(t)$, and acceleration $a(t)$. Because $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$ and $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, geometric features of higher-order curves dictate the values and profiles of lower-order curves: 1. **Slopes and rates:** The local slope of $x(t)$ defines the instantaneous value of $v(t)$, while the local slope of $v(t)$ defines $a(t)$. A horizontal segment (zero slope) in $x(t)$ yields $v = 0$; a linear slope in $x(t)$ yields a flat horizontal profile in $v(t)$ and $a = 0$; a parabolic curvature in $x(t)$ yields a linear ramp in $v(t)$ and a non-zero horizontal plateau in $a(t)$. 2. **Kinks and discontinuities:** A corner or kink in $v(t)$ (a sharp change in slope) corresponds to a step discontinuity in $a(t)$. 3. **Curvature and inflection points:** A point of inflection on a displacement or distance curve $x(t)$ occurs where the second derivative vanishes ($\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = 0$). Because this derivative is acceleration, an inflection point marks an extremum (peak or valley) of instantaneous velocity $v(t)$. ###### **Piecewise Constant-Acceleration Profile: The Ascending Elevator** Consider an elevator cab ascending along a vertical shaft, transitioning through three distinct phases: * **Initial acceleration ($t \in [1, 3]\text{ s}$):** The cab starts from rest at $x(1) = 0\text{ m}$. Velocity ramps linearly from $0$ to $4\text{ m/s}$, producing a constant positive acceleration $a = \frac{4 - 0}{3 - 1} = +2\text{ m/s}^2$. The position curve is a concave-upward parabola $x(t) = \frac{1}{2}(2)(t - 1)^2$, reaching $x(3) = 4.0\text{ m}$. * **Cruising phase ($t \in [3, 8]\text{ s}$):** Velocity remains strictly constant at $v = 4\text{ m/s}$. The slope of $v(t)$ is zero, causing acceleration to drop discontinuously to $a = 0\text{ m/s}^2$. Position evolves linearly as $x(t) = 4.0 + 4(t - 3)$, reaching $x(8) = 24.0\text{ m}$ at $t = 8\text{ s}$. * **Deceleration phase ($t \in [8, 9]\text{ s}$):** Braking reduces velocity from $4\text{ m/s}$ to $0\text{ m/s}$ over $\Delta t = 1\text{ s}$, yielding a negative slope $a = \frac{0 - 4}{9 - 8} = -4\text{ m/s}^2$. The position curve forms a concave-downward parabola flattening out at standstill ($v = 0$) at $t = 9\text{ s}$. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6.5 flowchart LR A["Position curve x(t)
Parabolic concave-up"] -->|"Slope dx/dt"| B["Velocity curve v(t)
Linear ramp upward"] B -->|"Slope dv/dt"| C["Acceleration a(t)
Positive plateau (+2)"] D["Position curve x(t)
Linear constant slope"] -->|"Slope dx/dt"| E["Velocity curve v(t)
Horizontal flat (4 m/s)"] E -->|"Slope dv/dt"| F["Acceleration a(t)
Zero level (0)"] G["Position curve x(t)
Parabolic concave-down"] -->|"Slope dx/dt"| H["Velocity curve v(t)
Linear ramp downward"] H -->|"Slope dv/dt"| I["Acceleration a(t)
Negative plateau (-4)"] ``` ###### **The Tangent Line Method for Mean and Instantaneous Velocities** For a particle moving rectilinearly from the origin ($S(0) = 0$), the running **mean velocity** $\bar{v}(t_0)$ over the interval $[0, t_0]$ is the secant slope from $(0,0)$ to the point $(t_0, S(t_0))$: $$\bar{v}(t_0) = \frac{S(t_0) - S(0)}{t_0 - 0} = \frac{S(t_0)}{t_0}$$ The **instantaneous velocity** at time $t_0$ is the tangent slope at that point: $$v(t_0) = \left.\frac{dS}{dt}\right|_{t=t_0}$$ The condition where instantaneous velocity equals running mean velocity, $v(t_0) = \bar{v}(t_0)$, is satisfied if and only if the tangent line to $S(t)$ at $t = t_0$ passes directly through the origin $(0, 0)$. Graphically, this time $t_0$ is located by anchoring a straight ray at the coordinate origin and rotating it until it forms a tangent to the experimental curve $S(t)$. ```{tikz} #| label: fig-tangent-secant #| fig-cap: "Identification of peak velocity at the inflection point and equality of instantaneous and mean velocity via the origin tangent ray." #| echo: false #| lang: tex #| fig-height: 3.5 \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, every node/.style={font=\small}] \draw[->] (-0.2,0) -- (6.5,0) node[right] {$t$}; \draw[->] (0,-0.2) -- (0,4.2) node[above] {$S(t)$}; % Sigmoidal curve \draw[thick, blue] (0,0) to[out=10, in=250] (2.8,1.6) to[out=70, in=190] (6,3.8); % Inflection point \filldraw[black] (2.8,1.6) circle (1.5pt); \draw[dashed, gray] (2.8,0) -- (2.8,1.6); \node[below] at (2.8,0) {$t_{\text{infl}}$}; \node[fill=white, inner sep=1pt] at (2.1,2.4) {$v_{\max} \text{ (inflection)}$}; % Tangency point from origin \filldraw[red] (3.8,2.7) circle (1.5pt); \draw[thick, red] (0,0) -- (5.3,3.76); \draw[dashed, red] (3.8,0) -- (3.8,2.7); \node[below, red] at (3.8,0) {$t_0$}; \node[fill=white, inner sep=1pt, text=red] at (4.5,1.5) {$v(t_0) = \bar{v}(t_0)$}; \end{tikzpicture} ``` On an S-shaped (sigmoidal) distance-time curve: * The point of maximum slope is the **inflection point** ($t_{\text{infl}}$), where the curve switches from concave upward ($\frac{d^2S}{dt^2} > 0$, speeding up) to concave downward ($\frac{d^2S}{dt^2} < 0$, slowing down). At this point, the instantaneous speed attains its absolute peak $v_{\max}$. * Because the slope decreases after the inflection point, the origin ray remains secant until it grazes the curve tangentially at $t_0 > t_{\text{infl}}$, identifying the unique moment where the current speed matches the cumulative average speed from departure. ###### **Extrema and Stationary Points: Worked Illustration** Kinematic curve features are verified analytically for a particle with position function: $$x(t) = 12t^2 - 2t^3 \quad (x\text{ in metres, } t\text{ in seconds})$$ Differentiating yields the velocity and acceleration functions: $$v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 24t - 6t^2 = 6t(4 - t)$$ $$a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 24 - 12t = 12(2 - t)$$ * **Stationary points and turnaround:** Setting $v(t) = 0$ yields $6t(4 - t) = 0$, giving rest instants at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and $t = 4\text{ s}$. The turnaround position (maximum positive coordinate) occurs at $t = 4\text{ s}$: $$x_{\max} = x(4) = 12(4)^2 - 2(4)^3 = 192 - 128 = 64\text{ m}$$ * **Acceleration at rest:** At the non-zero turnaround instant $t = 4\text{ s}$, the particle momentarily stops while accelerating back toward the origin: $$a(4) = 24 - 12(4) = -24\text{ m/s}^2$$ * **Maximum positive velocity:** The inflection point of $x(t)$ occurs when acceleration vanishes: $$a(t) = 24 - 12t = 0 \implies t = 2\text{ s}$$ Evaluating $v(t)$ at this time gives peak velocity: $$v_{\max} = v(2) = 24(2) - 6(2)^2 = 48 - 24 = 24\text{ m/s}$$ * **Instantaneous evaluation at $t = 3.0\text{ s}$:** $$x(3) = 12(3)^2 - 2(3)^3 = 108 - 54 = 54\text{ m}$$ $$v(3) = 24(3) - 6(3)^2 = 72 - 54 = 18\text{ m/s}$$ $$a(3) = 24 - 12(3) = 24 - 36 = -12\text{ m/s}^2$$ The mean velocity over $[0, 3]\text{ s}$ is $\bar{v} = \frac{x(3) - x(0)}{3 - 0} = \frac{54}{3} = 18\text{ m/s}$. Since $v(3) = \bar{v} = 18\text{ m/s}$, the secant from the origin to $(3, 54)$ is exactly tangent to $x(t)$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$.
